newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper not so unpopular, polls shows.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper not so unpopular, polls shows.

text.p: He may be scorned in Washington and be the target of repeated demands that he resign at home, but Colombian President Ernesto Samper is not all that unpopular, a poll showed on Monday.

The poll, conducted over the past two weeks by the National Consulting Centre, showed that 41 percent of Colombians still have a favourable opinion of Samper more than 2-1/2 years after he took office amid a snowballing drug corruption scandal.

That scandal, which has dogged Samper throughout his presidency and prompted repeated calls for his resignation, stems from charges that he knowingly received drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign.
The 41 percent approval rating is down just one percentage point from a survey conducted by the same consulting firm in December.

The lastest poll was conducted just before and after the United States "decertified" Colombia for a second year as a trustworthy ally in the drug war. Rather than sparking new calls for his resignation, diplomats say the U.S. move may actually have strengthened Samper's standing among some Colombians.

U.S. officials who argued in favour of decertification included U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard, who described Samper in testimony on Capitol Hill as as a "truly corrupt president who has a clear history of cooperating with drug dealers."

On a scale of one to five, Samper's government was given a three in the poll for its handling of the fight against Colombia's booming drug trade. But the rating dropped to a 2.7 for the government's management of ties with the United States and to 2.4 percent for its handling of corruption.

The public opinion poll was based on responses from 1,200 Colombians in 12 cities across the country and results were broadcast over the Caracol radio network. Its margin for error was plus or minus 3 percent.
